What we have now is a network of neural networks — each trained to recognize the next glyph. The process is far more advanced than in the original neural net; in addition to being capable of recognizing the next glyph in the current glyph-hour, each network can also recognize the next glyph in the previous glyph-hour. Moreover, the networks can take the next glyph in the previous glyph-hour as an input, and produce the next glyph in the current glyph-hour. In fact, the architecture has been extended to allow the current glyph-hour's network to receive as input a vector of the previous glyph-hours. This extended architecture enables the networks to learn the temporal dependencies between glyph-hours.
This was the first ever time that these neural nets were exposed to the task of learning the sequence of glyphs that make up a particular manuscript. After ten minutes of training they had memorized all the glyphs of the model's corpus, from beginning to end. The networks' performance was at a level that surprised even the model's creator.
The neural net was a very simple device — only five layers — and so was the model that it was trying to learn. Still, even with its modest complexity, the neural net had the ability to recognize and understand the model's glyphs. The human glyphs had been carefully selected for the model, and were clearly distinct from the surrounding glyphs. The neural nets' ability to learn, therefore, must be based on some type of semantic understanding.
This was the first time that the model's creator had observed the neural nets being exposed to an unseen corpus. It was also the first time the neural nets had the ability to learn a temporal sequence of glyphs. This meant that the neural nets had the ability to recognize the glyphs in the sequence from one glyph-hour to the next. It also meant that the model's creator would be able to understand the glyphs of the model and use the information to create other models. In fact, this was precisely what the creator had in mind when he designed the glyph-hour architecture. He wanted to be able to build models that are different, but related, to the model he had created.
In the next few years, the neural net architecture was refined. The new model could recognize glyphs in the next several glyph-hours of a manuscript. In addition, the model was trained on more and more glyphs at a time. By the end of that time, the model was able to memorize a large corpus of thousands of glyphs. The human glyphs in the model had become meaningless as the neural nets were able to recognize and learn them.</s>
